s13.slug: THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 18 · 4:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE STAIRS → 1:25 AM · 412 — LENA BACK
body: The sun has got low enough by half past four to come in under the lobby’s overhang and lie across the tile in a long yellow slant, with the shadow of the bike rack printed on it like a fence. Jack has his Anchor apron rolled up in one fist and his mail in the other: a letter from Ma with a coupon folded inside it for a Giant Eagle two thousand miles away, and a quarter sheet from Newman announcing Stations of the Cross, Fridays after the 12:10, in Becca’s handwriting with a little cross drawn over the *i* in *Fridays*. Down the wall of little brass doors, 217’s is where it always is, in the shade at the far end. He keeps his eyes on his own and his key in it.
Doug comes off the elevator in socks and a Tauren druid T-shirt with a party-size bag of Funyuns, sees him, and changes course.

“Dude.” He falls in beside Jack at the foot of the stairs. “Dude. Did you hear? Lena and the guitar guy. *Done.* Pete from his band told Priya’s friend’s roommate — it was, like, Valentine’s, by *text*, which is cold, dude, and now he’s playing all minor chords at the Bastille, like, on purpose —”
Jack keeps walking. Doug stays at the bottom with the Funyuns, still going — “which, musically, dude, is a *choice* —” — and the stairwell takes the rest and hands back only the echo.

From the third-floor landing the window gives him the curb. A black car with the trunk up. Laney comes down the front steps at a run, in socks, and stops a yard short of it like there’s a line painted on the concrete. Lena gets out of the back with a duffel on her shoulder and no pie box. When Laney gets her arms around her, Laney’s face is over Lena’s shoulder, toward the building: eyes shut tight, mouth pressed flat, the sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Jack is up the next flight before they’re through the doors.

At the Anchor he is very fast. Racks go into the Hobart and come out in a roll of steam and go up on the shelf still dripping; the stockpots are done by ten and the mats hosed by midnight, and at eleven Rudy says so from the flattop, like a complaint. “Slow down. There’s nothing left to wash.”

When he gets in, 412 is dark except for the streetlight, which comes through the blind and lays its bars up the wall and over the ceiling and finds Theo’s beads on the nail, gold and purple and a fogged green, hanging either side of the cross. Jack doesn’t hit the light. He comes in with the Hobart still on him — lemon sanitizer, hot rinse, the bottom of somebody’s clam chowder — and sits on the edge of his bed to get his shoes off. Across the room the closet door stands open on ten coats hung shoulder to shoulder in the dark, like a congregation that came early.
Theo is on his back with his hands folded on his chest, and his eyes are open. The streetlight is in them.
“She ended it with Julian. In New Orleans, last week. Her decision — nobody’s idea but hers.”
Jack gets the left shoe off and sets it by the footlocker, toe to the wall.

It’s information. It goes where he has been putting things since the first week of February, with the album he clicked past on Theo’s laptop and the empty chair at Hale’s and a black car with its trunk up this afternoon: other people’s weather, in other people’s cities. He starts on the right shoe. There’s a knot in the lace from the Anchor, wet and pulled tight, and he works at it with his thumbnail, and works at it, and then just pulls, and the lace snaps off in his hand down by the eyelet.

He sits there in the stripes holding the end of it, and for no reason he wants he thinks of Julian in the pew at the 11:30 since November with his hands folded, saying the responses half a line behind everybody else, learning them, and never going up. He puts that away with the rest.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Thursday there was a card in my box, cream, her mother’s, in her hand. Theo says I’m not coming. Her mother’s made up the twins’ room. American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat. I’d be welcome. At Hale’s we didn’t say a word to each other; everything went through the chair. After, I slid the card back down the table. She stopped it with two fingers before it went off the edge and put it in her bag. Thursday, February eighteenth, from the stairwell window: a car at the curb, Laney down the steps at a run, Lena out of the back with a duffel. Doug says she and the guitar guy are done. That night Theo told me in the dark: she ended it with Julian, in New Orleans, last week. Her decision. Nobody’s idea but hers.

choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you said okay.
response: A car goes by in the street below and drags the stripes off the ceiling and puts them back.
“Okay,” Theo says from his bed, in the same voice, as if the two of them have agreed on something.

choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you asked him why he was telling you.
response: “So you’d hear it from somebody who wasn’t Pruitt.”
Theo, who can talk for ten minutes about a lens, leaves it there. No pitch in it, no camera. It’s true, and he doesn’t dress it.

choices.text: “Tell Julian I’m sorry for his loss. On the good stock.”
choices.key: When Theo told you Lena ended it with Julian, you made a crack about Julian’s loss, on the good stock.
response: Theo says nothing for a long time. The beads on the nail catch the light from a car and let it go.
“I’m going to pretend I was asleep for that, Costigan.” The bedsprings go as he rolls toward the window, and that is the last of Theo for the night.

s13a.slug: FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 19 · 1:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOADING DOCK — LENT, DAY THREE

body.text: From the other bed, after a long time, while Jack is finding his shoes in the dark: “I’m not going to ask you which one.” And he doesn’t.
body.else: Theo’s breathing goes long and even in the other bed, asleep or giving a good impression of it, while Jack finds his shoes in the dark.

body: He takes the Carhartt off its hook by feel and goes down the back stairs with the shoes in his hand, the right one with its lace knotted together where it broke, and puts them on at the bottom on the cold concrete.

The dock at this hour belongs to the sodium lamp over the kitchen door, which makes everything under it the same orange: the dumpsters, the tower of milk crates, the bike racks with one stripped Huffy chained to them since September. Past the lot the eucalyptus is going in the wind off the lagoon, menthol and cat and rain that hasn’t come yet. The only other light on this side of the building is a window up on three with a Saints flag thumbtacked across it, hung on the seventh by somebody from Metairie and never taken down.

It comes up the back of his throat first, a Marlboro he hasn’t had: the paper, the first hot pull, as exact as the smell of a kitchen in another state. His hands find out after. They want the small business of it, the tap and the shake and the match cupped against the wind, and they have had nothing to do since Wednesday.

body.text: The pack is in the Carhartt where he put it Wednesday night, zipped in, and through the lining his fingers have found its corners and the soft give of the foil top on their own.

He has no pack. Osei has it, in a cassock pocket, up a hill, and would want a reason. At the bottom of the other hill the 7-Eleven sign is lit all night, red and green and orange, and from the end of the dock he can see the top of it over the roof of the parking structure.
The Folgers can is right there by his shoe, where it always is, and his pack is in it, under an inch of sand and somebody else’s butts.

body: In the right-hand pocket, against his hip, the tin.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Lent: no cigarettes. Two in the morning after the first Thursday of it, on the dock, I opened the tin and counted. Eleven.

response: The tin comes out warm from the pocket. The hinge gives with its small dry complaint, and under the orange light the cigarettes lie in their row.

He counts them with the tip of his little finger, one to eleven, and then back down from eleven to one, because a count that only goes one direction isn’t finished. Eleven. He shuts the lid and keeps the tin in his fist until his fist is warm again, and puts it back in the right-hand pocket.

He leaves his hands where they are, one on the corners of the pack and one on the tin, and stands under the lamp till they stop asking. It takes the eucalyptus going quiet and starting up again, twice.

One out of the soft pack, and a match from an Anchor book, cupped. The first drag goes down like a word he promised on a kneeler not to say. Lent, day three. He smokes it to the filter at the edge of the dock with the orange light on his hands, and doesn’t enjoy any of it except all of it.
He sits down on the edge of the dock with his feet hanging over the ramp and his hands under his thighs, and he stays there till the 7-Eleven is just a sign again.

Down the hill with his hands in his pockets. Five dollars and change, and a clerk eating sunflower seeds out of the bag who rings it up without lifting his eyes from a crossword. One, on the curb outside by the ice machine. The other nineteen go in the trash can beside it, which is the stupidest thing he has ever paid for.
He sets the side of his shoe against the can and keeps it there, a little pressure, the way you’d keep a door from blowing open, until he is cold enough to go back upstairs.

Two fingers in the sand. The pack comes up gritty and a little damp, and he lights one with sand still on the filter, and it tastes of the can, and he smokes it anyway, standing over the hole he made, down to nothing.

s20a.slug: MONDAY, FEBRUARY 22 · 1:00 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE END OF THE AFFAIR
body: The fog that came in off the Point at noon has stayed, and the light in the windows of 302 is the same flat white from the radiator to the clock. There’s no slab of sun on the varnish today. The table hasn’t got a bright end and a dark one. It has two ends.

The chairs have been rearranged by attrition. Caleb took the last seat at the window end on the eleventh, while it was empty and in the sun, and hasn’t given it back. “It has a better view of the door,” he says, to the table in general, when nobody has asked. That puts Lena two seats from the end, between Caleb and the window girl with the library copy that crackles. Yusuf has the corner and a lidded coffee. Evan has the roster and the radiator, and a Commons cup he holds in both hands for the heat. Jack has the door end and the clock, which is what he had before, and a used paperback from the campus bookstore, four dollars and fifty cents, with somebody else’s yellow highlighter all the way through the air raid and nowhere after it.

At the window end Lena has an old orange Penguin open flat under her left hand and a pencil in her right. She hasn’t looked down the table. He knows because he hasn’t either. She has been back four days: Thursday at the curb from a stairwell window, Sunday at the 11:30 on the Mary side, Sunday afternoon in the Fishbowl saying welcome back to somebody else. He has the list. He didn’t make it on purpose.

Hale comes in with his coat over his arm and his own copy bristling with torn strips of envelope, and takes the middle of the long side, where he can turn his head for either end. He turns it both ways, slowly, checking the traffic.

“The chair has had a restful fortnight,” he says, “and is ready to be shouted through again.” He lays the Greene on the roster. “Today, I’m reliably informed, is the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter. I take it as an endorsement of the method.”
“A load-bearing chair,” Yusuf says, into his coffee.
“Mr. Noorzai has the engineering of it. Rome has been resting a good deal of weight on a chair for some time, and it hasn’t given way yet, much as some of us have kicked at it.”
He gets up, uncaps a marker, and writes it in his tilted hand.

body.title: Whiteboard, Hollis 302
body.text: IS SARAH BOUND BY A VOW SHE MADE TO A GOD SHE DIDN’T BELIEVE IN?

body: “June of ’44,” Hale says, sitting down again. “A flying bomb. The front door comes off its hinges and down on top of Bendrix on the stairs, and Sarah finds him under it, and by every sign she has, he’s dead. So she goes back into the room and kneels on the floor, and she makes an offer to a God she has no grounds whatever to believe in: let him be alive, and she’ll give him up. And in walks Bendrix with plaster in his hair.” He opens his hands over the book. “She keeps it. That isn’t today’s question. Today’s question is whether she has to. The chair, for its part, is a Humean, and holds that a promise to a fiction binds nobody but the fiction. But the chair didn’t write the novel, and the man who did went to Mass. Miss Broussard. The chair.”

Lena answers Hale, not the table, in a voice pitched to reach the middle of the long side and stop there. Hale relays her half a sentence behind, reading it off her as she goes, so Jack gets all of it twice: first her vowels from the window end, low, not quite words at this distance, and then Hale’s, which carry.

“Miss Broussard says yes. She says a promise doesn’t wait until you deserve to have made it. Sarah keeps it because she said it, and keeping it is how she finds out who she said it to.” He checks with the window end. “Miss Broussard calls that the beginning of faith. Not” — another check — “the end of love.” He turns his head the long way round. “Mr. Costigan. The chair is listening, which it doesn’t do for just anybody.”
Yusuf writes something down. The library copy crackles.

Jack’s answer is there before Hale’s head has come back round to the door end. He didn’t have to go looking for it. It was there already, with an edge on it, and it got to the front of him faster than anything he read for today.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Gloria says he sat in the Anchor till two Sunday morning, reading her Housman. Thursday he made Lena and me speak only through him — all remarks to the chair. *Brideshead*: whether Julia’s right to send Charles away. He relayed every word. Lena’s gone two weeks, he says. I’ll have the table. February eleventh he relayed one of my remarks to her empty chair and caught himself. He finds he misses being contradicted. That night he took Evan to the Anchor for his thirtieth. February twenty-second she was back, and the chair rule stands. *The End of the Affair*: is Sarah bound by a vow she made to a God she didn’t believe in? She said yes, through him. I answered the same way.

choices.text: “Tell her Sarah keeps it because she’s afraid, not because she’s faithful.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you told Lena, through the chair, that Sarah keeps her vow out of fear, not faith.
response: Hale relays it down the varnish with the edges left on. Down the table Lena answers the open book in front of her, and Hale turns back with it.
“Miss Broussard says fear is where most people start. The ones who wait to be brave first never start at all.”
Hale sits back in his chair. “Rigor to Mr. Costigan,” he says, “heart to Miss Broussard, and the chair keeps the change.”

choices.text: “Tell her the vow is the best thing in the book.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you conceded, through the chair, that Sarah’s vow is the best thing in the book.
response: Hale relays it without a flourish. The pencil at the window end stops moving.
“Tell him thank you,” Lena says, to Hale.
“Miss Broussard says thank you.” Hale looks down the table one way and then the other, and folds his hands on the Greene. “The chair notes it has never been so frightened.”

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard that keeping a promise is easy when nobody’s on the other end of the line.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you told Lena, through the chair, that keeping a promise is easy when nobody’s on the other end of the line.
response: Hale relays it word for word, flatly and fast, holding it a little away from himself.

At the window end Lena finishes the line she was writing before she answers. This time her voice carries the length of the table, and Hale doesn’t bother to relay it. “Tell Mr. Costigan that Sarah keeps hers with Bendrix hating her for it the whole time. That’s the whole book.” The pencil goes down. “There’s always somebody on the other end of the line, Professor. Some people just stop picking up.”
Hale takes his hands off the Greene. “The chair declines to score that,” he says, “and would like a drink.”

choices.text: “The chair can tell her I pass.”
response: “Mr. Costigan passes,” Hale tells the window end. “The chair is shocked and recovering.”
At the far end the pencil moves. Whatever it writes, it doesn’t come down the table.
